n: Rachel, still childless, envies her sister and cries to Jacob in desperation. Her pain is real, though her demand is unfair.

f.w: Give me children, or else I die
f.g: Tragically, Rachel later dies giving birth to her second son (35:16-19).

n: Jacob angrily replies that he is not God—only God gives children. He is right, but his answer lacks compassion; contrast Isaac, who prayed for Rebekah.

f.g: “Am I in the place of God?”

n: Rachel offers her maid Bilhah, following the same custom Sarah used. A child born “upon her knees” would count as Rachel’s own.

f.g: A ritual of adoption: the child would be born onto Rachel’s lap and counted as hers.

f.w: that I may also have children by her

n: Rachel gives Bilhah to Jacob as a wife.

f.g: As a secondary wife; her children were full sons of Jacob.

n: Bilhah conceives and bears a son.
Rachel names him Dan, believing God has judged her case and heard her plea.
Bilhah bears a second son.
Rachel names him Naphtali, saying she has wrestled with her sister and won. The rivalry between the sisters is intense.
Leah, no longer having children, gives her maid Zilpah to Jacob as well. The competition escalates.
Zilpah bears a son.
Leah names him Gad, meaning good fortune.
Zilpah bears a second son.
Leah names him Asher, “happy,” saying women will call her blessed.
Reuben finds mandrakes during the wheat harvest and brings them to his mother. Rachel asks for some, likely believing they would help her conceive.

f.g: A plant with a fragrant fruit, believed in the ancient world to promote fertility (compare Song of Solomon 7:13).

n: Leah bitterly says Rachel has already taken her husband. Rachel strikes a bargain: Jacob will spend the night with Leah in exchange for the mandrakes.
Leah meets Jacob and tells him she has “hired” him for the night. The household’s rivalry is painfully on display.

f.g: Paid for; a wordplay on Issachar’s name in verse 18.

n: God listens to Leah, and she bears a fifth son. Ironically, it is Leah—who gave away the mandrakes—who conceives. Children come from God, not from charms.
Leah names him Issachar, meaning “reward” or “hire.”

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew “there is a reward (sakar).”

n: Leah bears a sixth son.
She names him Zebulun, hoping her husband will now honor or dwell with her. Leah still longs for Jacob’s love.

f.g: Sounds like Hebrew zaval, “to honor” or “to dwell.”

n: Leah also bears a daughter, Dinah. She is the only daughter named, because her story comes later (chapter 34).

f.g: Means “judgment” or “vindicated,” a feminine form related to Dan.

n: At last God remembers Rachel and answers her prayers. After years of waiting, her womb is opened.
Rachel bears a son and says God has taken away her shame. In that culture, childlessness was often wrongly seen as a disgrace.

She names him Joseph, praying the Lord will “add” another son. Joseph will become one of the Bible’s great heroes, and Latter-day Saints treasure the promises to his descendants, including the Nephites.

f.g: Means “may He add”; also sounds like “He has taken away.”

n: After Joseph’s birth—and the end of his fourteen years of service—Jacob asks Laban to let him go home.
Jacob asks for his wives and children, reminding Laban of his faithful service.

f.w: for whom I have served thee

n: Laban urges Jacob to stay, admitting he has learned through divination that the Lord blessed him because of Jacob.

f.g: Hebrew niḥashti—“I have learned by divination,” suggesting Laban used omens.

f.w: the LORD hath blessed me for thy sake

n: Laban invites Jacob to name his wages.
Jacob reminds Laban how faithfully he has worked and cared for his livestock.

f.w: how thy cattle was with me
f.g: How your herds fared under my care.

n: Laban’s small flock has multiplied under Jacob’s care. Now Jacob wants to build up his own household.
Jacob asks for no wages up front. He proposes a deal instead.

f.w: Thou shalt not give me any thing
f.g: Jacob asks for nothing in advance.

n: Jacob’s wages will be the unusually colored animals: speckled and spotted goats and dark sheep. Most sheep there were white and most goats dark, so this seemed a small share.

f.g: Animals with irregular coloring—normally a minority.

n: Jacob’s honesty will be easy to check: any plain-colored animal found in his flock could be counted as stolen.
Laban agrees eagerly, sure he is getting the better deal.

f.w: I would it might be according to thy word

n: That same day Laban secretly removes all the spotted and dark animals and gives them to his sons—cheating Jacob from the start.
Laban puts three days’ distance between his sons’ flocks and Jacob, so the spotted animals cannot breed with Jacob’s flock.

f.g: A long distance—perhaps 50 miles or more.

n: Jacob peels white stripes into branches of poplar, almond, and plane trees.

f.g: Peeled white stripes in the bark.
Probably almond (luz)—a wordplay with Bethel’s old name, Luz.

n: He places the striped branches at the watering troughs where the animals mated.
The flocks bear striped and spotted young. Ancient people believed what animals saw could affect their offspring; Jacob later credits God’s revelation, not the sticks, for the result (31:10-12).
Jacob separates his flock and positions Laban’s animals to face his striped ones, building up his own herds.

f.w: set the faces of the flocks
f.g: Arranged the flocks so they faced the striped animals.

n: Jacob uses the branches only when the strongest animals breed.
The weaker animals go to Laban and the stronger to Jacob. Jacob uses selective breeding to his advantage.
Jacob becomes very wealthy with flocks, servants, camels, and donkeys. Despite Laban’s schemes, God prospers Jacob as He promised at Bethel.
